cards.front: <mark>[…]</mark>: learning two cards together is harder than learning either alone.
cards.back: <mark>Interference</mark>: learning two cards together is harder than learning either alone.
cards.extra: e.g. vergeblich / erheblich — rhyme, similar shape, both keep lapsing.

cards.front: <mark>[…]</mark>: the front allows several answers but the back lists only one.
cards.back: <mark>Ambiguity</mark>: the front allows several answers but the back lists only one.
cards.extra: e.g. "great" → großartig or gewaltig. Either list every answer on the back, or add a constraint.

cards.front: <mark>[…]</mark>: the front does not say which question it is asking.
cards.back: <mark>Vagueness</mark>: the front does not say which question it is asking.
cards.extra: e.g. "Plato" → recite five factoids. One fact per card instead.

cards.front: Fix when no distinguisher is possible (true synonyms): a <mark>[…]</mark> in the cloze hint.
cards.back: Fix when no distinguisher is possible (true synonyms): a <mark>constraint</mark> in the cloze hint.
cards.extra: Artificial, so last resort. House shorthand: hint a = contains the letter a; -e = does not contain e.

cards.front: Powering through an ambiguous card teaches <mark>[…]</mark> (boldface, position, order) instead of the material.
cards.back: Powering through an ambiguous card teaches <mark>layout accidents</mark> (boldface, position, order) instead of the material.

cards.front: The one good reason to press Again: <mark>[…]</mark>.
cards.back: The one good reason to press Again: <mark>tried for a while and nothing came</mark>.
cards.extra: Bad reasons: interference, ambiguity, vagueness. Those are card bugs, not memory failures — mark the card.

cards.front: Broken card during review → <mark>[…]</mark>; fix later from the desktop.
cards.back: Broken card during review → <mark>mark it (<kbd>*</kbd>) and move on</mark>; fix later from the desktop.
cards.extra: anki bugs lists marked / flagged / leech notes. anki fix opens them.

cards.back: Redundancy: encode a fact <mark>in several contexts</mark>.
cards.extra: A word plus two example sentences; a conjugation table plus sentences using each form.

cards.front: Prefer <mark>[…]</mark> over front/back for algorithm steps, equation terms, conjugations and lines of code.
cards.back: Prefer <mark>cloze</mark> over front/back for algorithm steps, equation terms, conjugations and lines of code.

cards.front: One <mark>[…]</mark> per card. A note may spawn several cards, but each card asks exactly one thing.
cards.back: One <mark>fact</mark> per card. A note may spawn several cards, but each card asks exactly one thing.

cards.front: A <mark>[…]</mark> (a card that keeps lapsing) is usually a card bug: interference or ambiguity, not a memory problem.
cards.back: A <mark>leech</mark> (a card that keeps lapsing) is usually a card bug: interference or ambiguity, not a memory problem.
cards.extra: This collection tags leeches after 5 lapses. Treat the tag as a bug report.

cards.front: Fix for interference: a <mark>[…]</mark> — one cloze note that teaches the contrast itself.
cards.back: Fix for interference: a <mark>distinguisher</mark> — one cloze note that teaches the contrast itself.
cards.extra:
{{c1::e}}r{{c1::h}}eblich: {{c2::considerable}}
{{c1::ve}}r{{c1::g}}eblich: {{c2::in vain}} — the wrong word becomes a trigger for the right one.

cards.front: Rule of three: 0 events in n trials → a quick 95% upper bound on the rate is <mark>[…]</mark>.
cards.back: Rule of three: 0 events in n trials → a quick 95% upper bound on the rate is <mark>3 / n</mark>.
cards.extra: Exact two-sided Clopper–Pearson gives ≈ 3.69 / n. So 0/87 → about 4.2%, i.e. 1 in 24.

cards.front: To defend a 1-in-272 error rate (0.37%) with zero observed errors you need about <mark>[…]</mark> clean trials.
cards.back: To defend a 1-in-272 error rate (0.37%) with zero observed errors you need about <mark>1,000</mark> clean trials.

cards.front: Bonferroni: with m tests, reject only when p < <mark>[…]</mark>.
cards.back: Bonferroni: with m tests, reject only when p < <mark>α / m</mark>.
cards.extra: Controls family-wise error. Conservative when tests are correlated.

cards.front: Minimum detectable effect shrinks with <mark>[…]</mark>: quadrupling n halves it.
cards.back: Minimum detectable effect shrinks with <mark>√n</mark>: quadrupling n halves it.
cards.extra: mcp-tool-selection-eval at n = 44 has an MDE of ~17 percentage points.

cards.front: A leaderboard rank order from one eval run is a <mark>[…]</mark>. Ask what fraction of bootstrap resamples reproduce it.
cards.back: A leaderboard rank order from one eval run is a <mark>point estimate</mark>. Ask what fraction of bootstrap resamples reproduce it.
cards.extra: mcp-tool-selection-eval: the published order reproduced 24% of the time.

cards.front: When every model sees the same items, analyze <mark>[…]</mark> differences: item variance cancels.
cards.back: When every model sees the same items, analyze <mark>paired</mark> differences: item variance cancels.
cards.extra: yt-tldr-eval: only "Haiku is worst" survives the paired analysis.

cards.front: Bean et al. (NeurIPS 2025) audited 445 AI benchmarks; only <mark>[…]</mark> did any statistical testing.
cards.back: Bean et al. (NeurIPS 2025) audited 445 AI benchmarks; only <mark>16%</mark> did any statistical testing.

cards.front: Items every model gets right, or every model gets wrong, carry <mark>[…]</mark> for ranking.
cards.back: Items every model gets right, or every model gets wrong, carry <mark>zero information</mark> for ranking.
cards.extra: 14 of 44 items in mcp-tool-selection-eval; 0 separate #1 from #2.
